title: Apple One and Apple TV subscription prices increase by up to 20 percent
gist: Apple raised Apple TV and Apple One subscription prices by up to 20%, continuing a pattern of annual increases as Apple leans harder on its high-margin services segment and tries to push its long-unprofitable, reportedly billion-dollar-a-year-losing streaming service toward profitability.

insights.claim: Apple raised its Apple TV monthly subscription by $2 to $15, and its annual subscription by 20% from $99 to $119, effective immediately, with current subscribers getting one month's notice before the new price applies.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Direct revenue-per-subscriber uplift for Apple's services segment; a 20% annual-plan increase is unusually steep and signals management is now prioritizing monetization over subscriber growth for this product.
insights.locator: Apple increased the price for a monthly subscription

insights.claim: This marks a continued pattern of near-annual Apple TV price hikes: from $5/month at 2019 launch, to $10 in 2022, to $13 in August 2025, and now $15 in August 2026, with additional increases also occurring in October 2022 and October 2023.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: The pricing trajectory shows Apple TV has tripled in price in roughly seven years, a clear and repeatable monetization pattern investors can use to model future services-revenue growth assumptions.
insights.locator: Apple’s most recent price hike was in August 2025

insights.claim: Apple also raised the individual Apple One bundle (which includes Apple TV, Arcade, Fitness+, Music, News+, and iCloud+) from $20 to $22/month, following last month's Apple Music price increase from $11 to $13, and last month's hikes to Apple One's Family plan (from $26 to $28) and Premier plan (from $38 to $40).
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A coordinated, multi-tier bundle price escalation across nearly all Apple One plans within roughly a month indicates a systematic services repricing initiative rather than isolated adjustments, a stronger signal for near-term services revenue growth than a single price change would be.
insights.locator: Apple also increased the cost of a monthly individual subscription

insights.claim: In the quarter ending June 27, services represented 28.1% of Apple's revenue versus 71.9% from hardware, but services carry a much lower cost of sales (13.7%) compared to hardware (86.3%), making services disproportionately more profitable per dollar of revenue.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Quantifies why Apple is incentivized to keep raising services prices: services margins vastly exceed hardware margins, so shifting revenue mix toward services (via price hikes, not just subscriber growth) directly boosts blended gross margin — a core thesis for Apple's stock bulls.

insights.claim: The Information reported in 2025, citing an anonymous employee, that Apple TV was Apple's only unprofitable services offering and wasn't expected to become profitable for at least its first ten years, with another anonymous source claiming the service was losing more than $1 billion annually.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A concrete (if unverified/leaked) loss figure — over $1 billion/year — gives investors a specific magnitude for how much content spending is dragging on Apple's otherwise high-margin services business, and explains the strategic urgency behind repeated price hikes.

insights.claim: Apple originally positioned Apple TV as a low-priced pathway to sell other Apple hardware and services rather than a standalone profit center, but the author argues it's now reasonable for Apple to expect more direct returns from the service.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Signals a strategic pivot from loss-leader/ecosystem-lock-in framing toward direct profitability targets for Apple TV, which could mean continued price increases and/or content-spend discipline ahead.

insights.claim: Apple TV remains cheaper than Netflix's ad-free plan ($20/month) and Disney+'s ad-free plan ($19/month) and carries no ads, but has a much smaller content library than those larger rivals.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Apple still has room to raise Apple TV prices further before reaching rough price parity with Netflix/Disney+, though its smaller library is a competitive weakness that limits pricing power and subscriber growth relative to peers.
insights.locator: Apple TV doesn’t have commercials and is still cheaper

insights.claim: The author notes that without an ad-supported tier, small incremental price hikes are the simplest lever for Apple TV to drive revenue, but this approach risks undermining subscriber growth, another path to the same goal.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Frames the core strategic tradeoff investors should watch: price increases boost near-term ARPU but could suppress subscriber growth, so future subscriber-count trends will be the key metric to gauge whether this pricing strategy is working.
